mari_keremet.name: curses and afflicts those who break ritual or commit wrong
mari_keremet.notes: As the adversary-power and lord of earth and water, Keremet records human misdeeds and ritual violations and visits sickness and misfortune in return; his wrath must be turned aside by sacrifice.

sources.reference: L. S. Toidybekova, 'The Character of Keremet in the Mari Religion' (Folklore: Electronic Journal of Folklore)

mari_kugu_yumo.name: creates the world and decrees the laws of the universe
mari_kugu_yumo.notes: Supreme good god of Mari henotheism; mythological creator of the laws of the cosmos and protector of mankind, of whom the lesser deities are manifestations.

sources.reference: Uno Harva (Holmberg), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (Mythology of All Races IV)

marind_sami.name: stands among the first dema brought forth by sky and earth
marind_sami.notes: Sami is named beside Geb as a child of the sky-dema Dinadin and earth-dema Nubog in the Marind cosmogony; with the other primal dema he belongs to the generation from which the ancestral clans descend.

sources.reference: Jan van Baal, Dema: Description and Analysis of Marind-anim Culture (South New Guinea), 1966

marquesan_mahuike.name: holds the fire of the lower world in his body
marquesan_mahuike.notes: Keeper of fire in the Po; from him the culture-hero Mahui (his grandson) wins fire for humankind by stratagem.

sources.reference: E. S. C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (Bernice P. Bishop Museum Bulletin 69, 1930)
Mari religion, in Encyclopedia.com (Mari and Mordvin Religion)
Uno Harva (Holmberg), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (Mythology of All Races IV)

marind_geb.gloss: the coconut-dema (his body yields the first coconut palm)

maya_ah_puch.name: collar of disembodied eyes on their nerve-cords

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)
Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

maya_hunahpu.name: rubber ball of the Xibalba ballgame

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

mari_keremet.name: propitiatory sacrifice at the keremet grove
mari_keremet.notes: Each locality kept a separate keremet cult-place — a grove distinct from the groves of the good gods — where dark-coloured animals were sacrificed to appease Keremet and turn aside affliction.

sources.reference: L. S. Toidybekova, 'The Character of Keremet in the Mari Religion' (Folklore: Electronic Journal of Folklore)
'Keremet', Encyclopaedia Britannica

mari_kugu_yumo.name: communal grove sacrifice led by the kart priest
mari_kugu_yumo.cadence: seasonal communal prayers (some twenty a year)
mari_kugu_yumo.notes: Public prayers and animal sacrifices to the supreme god are held in the sacred groves (küsoto), the kart priest lighting the ceremonial fire, choosing the victims, blessing the offerings and reciting the prayers; no temples or central clergy.

sources.reference: Mari religion, in Encyclopedia.com (Mari and Mordvin Religion)
'Kart', Encyclopaedia Britannica

mari_mlande_ava.name: earth-mother grove offering
mari_mlande_ava.notes: As mother of the soil and the womb, Mlande-Ava received grove offerings and prayers for the fertility of fields and the safe quickening of children within the general Mari grove cult.

sources.reference: Uno Harva (Holmberg), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (Mythology of All Races IV)

mari_shochyn_ava.name: offering for conception and safe birth
mari_shochyn_ava.cadence: on seeking or expecting a child
mari_shochyn_ava.notes: Women seeking or carrying a child prayed and made offerings to the birth-mother Shochyn-Ava at the fir-branch altar by the sacred tree.

sources.reference: Mari religion, Wikipedia (Shochyn-Ava, goddess of childbirth)

mari_tul_ava.name: hearth-fire offering to the fire-mother
mari_tul_ava.cadence: at the hearth and at grove sacrifices
mari_tul_ava.notes: The fire-mother who keeps the hearth pure received offerings cast into the fire, and the kindling of the ceremonial sacrificial fire belonged to her sphere.

sources.reference: Uno Harva (Holmberg), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (Mythology of All Races IV)

marind_sosom.name: Sosom initiation cult
marind_sosom.notes: In the Sosom cult the coming of the giant dema, announced by the roaring bullroarer, framed the seclusion and initiation of the young men, from which the women were driven off; the rite is bound up with the ritualized homosexuality of Marind male initiation.

sources.reference: Jan van Baal, Dema: Description and Analysis of Marind-anim Culture (South New Guinea), 1966
Paul Wirz, Die Marind-anim von Holländisch-Süd-Neu-Guinea (1922-25)

marquesan_tanaoa.name: fishermen's offerings to the sea-god
marquesan_tanaoa.notes: Demoted from the primeval paramountcy, Tana'oa survived in cult as god of the sea, winds and fishing, receiving the invocations and offerings of fishermen as Te Fatu Moana, Lord of the Sea.

sources.reference: E. S. C. Handy, The Native Culture in the Marquesas (Bishop Museum Bulletin 9, 1923)

marquesan_tiki.name: veneration of carved tiki images at the me'ae
marquesan_tiki.notes: Wood and stone ti'i images, some up to ten feet high, representing the first man and the deified ancestors, were set up at the me'ae (sacred precincts) as foci of worship.

sources.reference: E. S. C. Handy, The Native Culture in the Marquesas (Bishop Museum Bulletin 9, 1923)

maya_chaac.name: Ch'a-Cháak rain-petition ceremony
maya_chaac.cadence: in drought / before the planting season
maya_chaac.notes: A community rain rite still performed in Yucatán: the h-men sets out a four-cornered altar with directional offerings and a ceremonial banquet, four boys at the corners croak as frogs, and invocations are chanted to the four directional Chaacs to 'fetch the rain'.

sources.reference: E. F. Flores & Balam, 'Importance of Plants in the Ch'a Chaak Maya Ceremony' (Journal of Ethnobiology 17:1, 1997)
Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

maya_itzamna.name: New-Year rites of the priesthood
maya_itzamna.notes: As patron of priests, scribes and healing, Itzamna was honoured in priestly festivals — notably the rites of the month Uo, when the ah kin opened and consulted the sacred books under his patronage.

sources.reference: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

maya_ix_chel.name: pilgrimage to the oracle-shrine of Cozumel
maya_ix_chel.notes: Maya women crossed by canoe to the island shrine of Ix Chel on Cozumel to petition for fertility, safe childbirth and healing; Landa records the well-trodden pilgrim roads and the oracle whose hollow-backed idol spoke through a concealed priest.

sources.reference: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

maya_kinich_ahau.name: solar cult of Izamal (Kinich Kakmó)
maya_kinich_ahau.notes: At Izamal the sun was venerated as Kinich Kakmó ('Fiery/Sun-eyed Macaw'), said to descend to the temple at the zenith to consume the offerings burned for him.

sources.reference: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

maya_kukulkan.name: festival of Kukulkán in the month Xul
maya_kukulkan.notes: Landa records a great festival of Kukulkán held at Maní in the month Xul (16 Xul), with fasting, processions and the descent of the god, drawing worshippers from across Yucatán; at Chichén Itzá his temple is the great pyramid down which the equinox shadow-serpent descends.

sources.reference: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán

maya_tohil.name: blood-sacrifice for the gift of fire
maya_tohil.cadence: continual; with captives taken in war
maya_tohil.notes: Patron god of the K'iche', Tohil gave fire to the tribes only in return for blood; his cult demanded the offering of the worshippers' own blood and the hearts of captives sacrificed before his image, the charter of human sacrifice in K'iche' tradition.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)
Francisco Ximénez, Historia de la provincia de San Vicente de Chiapa y Guatemala

sacredPlants.name: the trees of the sacred grove (küsoto)
sacredPlants.notes: Worship is offered in standing groves of old trees rather than built temples; the grove itself is the sanctuary of the supreme god.

sources.reference: Mari religion, in Encyclopedia.com (Mari and Mordvin Religion)

sacredAnimals.name: horse / foal
sacredAnimals.notes: The horse was the prime sacrificial animal of the great Mari grove-feasts.

sources.reference: Uno Harva (Holmberg), Finno-Ugric and Siberian Mythology (Mythology of All Races IV)

sacredPlants.name: coconut palm
sacredPlants.notes: Marind myth equates the coconut with the human head; the first coconut palm sprang from the body of Geb.

sources.reference: Jan van Baal, Dema: Description and Analysis of Marind-anim Culture, 1966

attributes.name: towering giant wearing a string of enemy heads
attributes.notes: Sosom is imagined as a gigantic dema, his approach signalled by the whirring of the bullroarer.

sources.reference: Jan van Baal, Dema: Description and Analysis of Marind-anim Culture, 1966

attributes.name: squat large-headed anthropomorphic ti'i figure
attributes.notes: Carved in wood and stone with a massive rounded head, large eyes and hands on belly; the canonical Marquesan ti'i form representing the first man and the ancestors.

sources.reference: E. S. C. Handy, The Native Culture in the Marquesas (Bishop Museum Bulletin 9, 1923)

attributes.name: skeletal or bloated putrefying body hung with death-bells
attributes.notes: God A appears either as a skeleton with exposed spine and skull or as a bloated decomposing corpse, wearing bells and a collar of eyes.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredAnimals.name: moan bird (screech owl)
sacredAnimals.notes: The moan owl is his death-omen bird; the dog serves as guide of the dead to Xibalba.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

attributes.name: long pendulous up-curled snout and serpentine fangs
attributes.notes: God B is shown with a reptilian face, a long down-curving nose, scrolled eyes and shell ear-ornaments, brandishing a lightning-axe or serpents.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredAnimals.name: frog / toad
sacredAnimals.notes: Frogs (uo) are the heralds and musicians of the rains; boys impersonate them croaking at the corners of the Ch'a-Cháak altar.

sources.reference: E. F. Flores & Balam, 'Importance of Plants in the Ch'a Chaak Maya Ceremony' (Journal of Ethnobiology 17:1, 1997)

attributes.name: aged toothless face with great curved nose and squint eyes
attributes.notes: God D is an old man with sunken cheeks, a single tooth and a square beard, often crowned with the Principal Bird Deity headdress.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredAnimals.name: Principal Bird Deity (Itzam-Ye)
sacredAnimals.notes: His celestial bird manifestation perches atop the World Tree.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

attributes.name: coiled serpent worn in the hair
attributes.notes: Her aged Chak Chel aspect (Goddess O) bears a serpent headdress, jaguar ears and claws, and an overturned water-jar from which the flood pours.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredAnimals.name: rabbit (in the moon)
sacredAnimals.notes: The lunar rabbit is her companion, sometimes shown weaving or seated in her lap; she is the moon goddess.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

attributes.name: squared crossed eyes, T-shaped filed teeth and the k'in sign
attributes.notes: God G has large squint or crossed eyes, a Roman nose, a beard, filed front teeth and the k'in (sun) sign on brow or body.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredAnimals.name: jaguar
sacredAnimals.notes: By night the sun becomes the Jaguar God of the underworld; at Izamal the solar bird is the fiery macaw, Kinich Kakmó.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

attributes.name: elongated tonsured head like a maize cob, jade-adorned
attributes.notes: Identified with the Tonsured Maize God (Hun Nal Ye): an idealized youth with a cleft, foliated head and net-skirt, shown reborn rising from a cracked turtle carapace.

sources.reference: Karl Taube, The Major Gods of Ancient Yucatan (Dumbarton Oaks, 1992)

sacredPlants.name: maize
sacredPlants.notes: His death and rebirth model the maize cycle; his severed head set in a calabash tree fruits as the gourd that quickens Lady Blood.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

sacredPlants.name: calabash (gourd) tree
sacredPlants.notes: His skull hung in a calabash tree spat into Xquic's hand.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

attributes.name: black corpse-spots on the skin
attributes.notes: The elder Hero Twin (often the Headband/God S figure) is marked with black spots, complementing his brother Xbalanque's jaguar patches.

sources.reference: Michael D. Coe, The Hero Twins: Myth and Image (in The Maya Vase Book)

sacredAnimals.name: birds of the blowgunner
sacredAnimals.notes: As Hun-Ahpu, 'One Blowgunner', he is the hunter of birds; with the blowgun he downs Vucub Caquix from the nance tree.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

attributes.name: leaf-nosed bat with a knife-like snout
attributes.notes: A therianthropic death-bat, human-bodied with bat head and wings and a cutting flint snout, ruler of the House of Bats (Zotzilá).

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

sacredAnimals.name: bat
sacredAnimals.notes: The bat is his namesake and his hosts in Xibalba.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

attributes.name: serpent sheathed in blue-green quetzal feathers
attributes.notes: Afloat on the primal sea wrapped in quetzal plumes; among the K'iche' he also takes the forms of eagle and jaguar and even a pool of blood.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

sacredAnimals.name: resplendent quetzal
sacredAnimals.notes: His name q'uq' is the quetzal; the bird's green plumage marks the feathered serpent.

sources.reference: Popol Vuh (trans. Allen J. Christenson)

sacredAnimals.name: bear
sacredAnimals.notes: As first-born son of the West Wind and guardian of tradition and ceremony, Maajiigawiz is associated in Anishinaabe story with the bear.

sources.reference: Basil Johnston, Ojibway Heritage (1976)
